The Senate on Wednesday ordered an investigation into alleged arbitrary airtime deductions by telecommunications operators for failed, dropped and prematurely terminated calls, giving its Committee on Communications four weeks to establish the financial losses suffered by subscribers. The resolution followed a motion on consumer protection in the telecommunications sector, which highlighted persistent complaints by Nigerians over deductions for calls that fail to connect, terminate abruptly or are disrupted by poor network services. The motion was sponsored by the Chief Whip of the Senate, Senator Tahir Monguno, and presented by the Deputy Senate Leader. It was seconded by Senator Ned Nwoko, representing Delta North, who described the problem as one affecting virtually every telecommunications subscriber in the country. Supporting the motion, Nwoko said the proposed investigation was necessary to protect consumers from avoidable financial losses arising from poor service delivery by network operators. “This is a well-thought-out motion. It is very straightforward. It is all about consumer protection. We need to make this particular motion at this critical time because a lot of the time, everybody is involved in the use of calls, making calls across the country, and we all experience the same technical issues,” he said. However, during consideration of the prayers, the Deputy Minority Leader proposed that the Senate adopt only Prayer Six, arguing that it sufficiently captured the issues raised in the preceding five prayers. Reading the resolution, Akpabio said the Committee on Communications had been directed to invite the Nigerian Communications Commission and relevant telecommunications operators to investigate complaints concerning failed calls, dropped calls, unterminated calls and inflated charges. The committee is also expected to establish the financial losses incurred by subscribers and submit its findings, alongside recommendations for further legislative and regulatory action, within four weeks. The consolidated resolution brings under one investigation several proposals seeking an inquiry into the billing practices of MTN Nigeria, Globacom, Airtel and T2 Mobile; the establishment of an accessible complaints and redress mechanism; automatic refunds for verifiably failed calls; independent technical audits of billing systems; and stricter enforcement of quality-of-service standards. Speaking after the adoption, Akpabio urged the Committee on Communications, chaired by Senator Bill Bills, to commence work immediately, describing the four-week deadline as lengthy but necessary. Four weeks is too long, but we can allow it. If in four weeks they don’t satisfy us, then we have to take it as a Committee of the Whole and invite all the operators, in addition to the Minister overseeing the NCC and also the Executive Vice Chairman of NCC, to ask these pertinent questions,” he said. The Senate President said the growing complaints from telecommunications subscribers could no longer be ignored, particularly as consumers continued to lose money over services that were either poorly delivered or not provided at all. “The public is complaining, and our job here is to make sure that we tackle the concerns of the Nigerian public and also the losses they suffer that are actually avoidable,” he said. Akpabio also expressed concern that inadequate supervision might be contributing to the persistent problems in the sector, stressing the need to engage the NCC, the supervising minister and telecommunications operators to ensure accountability and lasting improvements. The probe is expected to determine the extent of subscribers’ financial losses, establish whether operators have complied with existing regulatory requirements on billing transparency and quality of service, and identify possible gaps in the enforcement of consumer protection rules. Telecommunications subscribers have repeatedly complained about losing airtime when calls fail to connect, disconnect shortly after connection or are interrupted by network problems. Such complaints have raised questions about the fairness and transparency of operators’ billing systems, particularly where subscribers are charged despite receiving little or no service. The Senate’s intervention is therefore aimed at establishing whether the deductions are attributable to technical failures, billing-system deficiencies or regulatory lapses, and determining the appropriate remedies for affected consumers. The committee’s report is expected to provide the basis for possible legislative and regulatory measures, including improved monitoring of operators, more effective complaint-resolution mechanisms and refunds where wrongful deductions are established. Akpabio’s warning also signals the possibility of a wider legislative inquiry involving the NCC, the supervising minister and the affected operators if the committee fails to deliver within four weeks.
